SHORT NOTES
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

sections.title: Nature of Diversity in Indian Society
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Indian society is marked by great diversity in language, religion, caste, tribe, region, customs and ways of life. This diversity has developed through a long historical process. Diversity does not mean complete separation; different communities interact within common political, economic and cultural institutions.

Census 2011 recorded 1,210.8 million people in India, divided into many religious groups. Hindus formed about 79.8 per cent of the population, Muslims about 14.2 per cent, Christians about 2.3 per cent and Sikhs about 1.7 per cent, with Buddhists, Jains and others making up the rest. The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution recognizes 22 languages, and the census recorded hundreds of mother tongues.
The main forms of diversity are:
- racial or ethnic diversity (B.S. Guha classified the Indian population into six main racial elements),
- linguistic diversity (Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic and Tibeto-Burman language families),
- religious diversity,
- caste and tribal diversity,
- regional and geographical diversity,
- cultural diversity in food, dress, festivals, music and art.

Mizoram adds to this diversity. Its population is mostly Scheduled Tribe and Christian, its main language (Mizo) belongs to the Tibeto-Burman family, and the state has customs and institutions distinct from those of the plains of India.

sections.title: Forces of Unity
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Unity in India is supported by a shared constitutional framework, political institutions, historical interaction, economic interdependence, communication, national movements and common civic values. These forces help different groups live within a single social and political order.
The bonds of unity include:
- geographical unity, with natural boundaries formed by the Himalayas and the seas;
- political unity under one Constitution, one citizenship and a common parliamentary system;
- religious and cultural interaction, such as pilgrimages across the country, the Bhakti and Sufi movements, and shared festivals;
- linguistic links through Hindi and English as link languages;
- economic interdependence;
- the shared experience of the national freedom movement.

Sociologists have described Indian culture as showing 'unity in diversity'. Historians such as Radha Kumud Mookerji wrote about the 'fundamental unity of India', and Jawaharlal Nehru, in 'The Discovery of India', spoke of an underlying unity that made the many diversities part of one civilization.

Modern forces of unity include the national media, railways, roads and air transport, national sports, cinema, the armed forces, all-India services and educational institutions that bring together students from all regions.

sections.title: Multiculturalism
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Multiculturalism recognizes the existence and value of different cultural communities within the same society. In India it is visible in the coexistence of many languages, religions, customs and ethnic traditions. It emphasizes respect for diversity while maintaining a common civic framework.

Multiculturalism is both a social fact (the presence of many cultures) and a policy (official recognition and protection of cultural diversity). It is opposed to the 'melting pot' model, in which minorities are expected to give up their culture, and is often compared to a 'salad bowl' or 'mosaic', in which different cultures keep their identity.
The Indian Constitution supports multiculturalism through several provisions:
- Articles 29 and 30, which protect the cultural and educational rights of minorities;
- the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, which protect tribal areas;
- special provisions such as Article 371G for Mizoram.

Challenges to multiculturalism include communalism, regionalism, linguistic conflicts and pressures towards cultural uniformity. Supporters argue that recognizing diversity strengthens unity by making all groups feel included.

sections.title: Forces of National Integration
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: National integration refers to the development of unity and common belonging among diverse groups. The Constitution, democratic institutions, education, communication, economic links and respect for cultural diversity are important forces of national integration.

The National Integration Council was set up in 1961 to address problems such as communalism, casteism, regionalism and linguism. It brings together national and state leaders to discuss threats to unity.
Obstacles to national integration include:
- communalism and caste conflicts;
- regionalism and demands based on narrow regional loyalties;
- linguistic disputes;
- economic inequality between regions;
- insurgency in some border areas;
- the misuse of identity in politics.
Measures to promote integration include:
- value education;
- balanced regional development;
- protecting minority and tribal rights;
- cultural exchange programmes such as Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat;
- national symbols and celebrations;
- peaceful settlement of disputes through dialogue and accords, as with the Mizo Peace Accord of 1986.

sections.title: Tribal Segment of Indian Society
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Tribal communities form an important segment of Indian society. They possess varied languages, cultural traditions, social organizations and relationships with land and natural resources. Their social conditions differ widely across regions.

Census 2011 recorded about 10.4 crore Scheduled Tribe people, about 8.6 per cent of India's population. More than 700 communities are notified as Scheduled Tribes. In Mizoram, Scheduled Tribes make up about 94 per cent of the population.
Common features of tribal communities, as described by sociologists, are:
- a definite territory;
- a common name and dialect;
- strong kinship ties and clan organization;
- a relatively simple economy based on shifting cultivation, hunting, gathering or settled agriculture;
- their own religious beliefs;
- customary laws and political institutions such as village councils or chiefs.

However, many tribal communities today are highly literate and urbanized, and the old picture of the 'isolated tribe' does not fit all groups. Mizoram, for example, has one of the highest literacy rates in India (91.3 per cent in Census 2011).

sections.title: Agrarian Segment
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: The agrarian segment is connected with agriculture and rural life. Land relations, caste, class, kinship and village institutions have historically shaped agrarian society in India.
Agrarian social structure in India has traditionally been described in terms of three groups:
- landlords, such as zamindars;
- owner-cultivators or peasants;
- tenants, sharecroppers and agricultural labourers.
Daniel Thorner used the terms 'malik', 'kisan' and 'mazdur' for these groups.
Land reforms after independence included:
- abolition of the zamindari system;
- tenancy reforms;
- land ceiling laws;
- consolidation of holdings.
The Green Revolution of the 1960s increased production in states such as Punjab and Haryana, but it also widened inequality between large and small farmers.
Agriculture still employs a large share of India's workforce, but its share of national income has declined. Problems of the agrarian segment include:
- small and fragmented holdings;
- indebtedness;
- dependence on the monsoon;
- low prices for produce;
- farmer distress.

sections.title: Industrial Segment
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Industrial society develops around factory production, wage labour, urban centres and modern occupations. Industrialization changes class relations, family life, migration and patterns of social interaction.
Industrialization in India began under colonial rule with:
- the cotton mills of Bombay;
- the jute mills of Bengal;
- the railways;
- the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur (founded 1907).
After independence, planned industrialization through the Five Year Plans built heavy industries in the public sector. Liberalization in 1991 opened the economy to private and foreign investment.
Social consequences of industrialization include:
- urbanization and migration from villages to cities;
- the growth of a working class and a middle class;
- trade unions;
- the decline of hereditary occupations;
- the growth of nuclear families;
- secularization of outlook;
- new problems such as slums, pollution and industrial disputes.
A large part of the Indian workforce is in the unorganized or informal sector, without job security or social security. This is an important feature of the Indian industrial segment.

sections.title: Village Community
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: The village has historically been an important unit of Indian rural society. Village life is shaped by agriculture, kinship, caste, local institutions and patterns of cooperation and dependence. Modern education, markets, migration and government programmes have transformed village society.

In 1830, Sir Charles Metcalfe described Indian villages as 'little republics', almost self-sufficient and unchanging. Later sociologists such as M.N. Srinivas and S.C. Dube criticized this view. They showed that villages were linked to towns, markets and the state, and that villages had internal inequality.
Important village studies include:
- S.C. Dube's 'Indian Village' (1955), a study of Shamirpet near Hyderabad;
- M.N. Srinivas's study of Rampura in Mysore, later published as 'The Remembered Village' (1976);
- McKim Marriott's 'Village India' (1955), which used the concepts of 'universalization' and 'parochialization'.
Changes in villages include:
- Panchayati Raj under the 73rd Amendment (1992);
- rural development schemes;
- roads and electricity;
- mobile phones;
- migration;
- the decline of the jajmani system.
In Mizoram, villages are governed by elected Village Councils under the Lushai Hills District (Village Councils) Act, 1953.

sections.title: Jajmani System
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: The Jajmani system was a traditional arrangement of hereditary exchange of goods and services between caste groups in many Indian villages. Service groups provided specialized services to landholding or patron families in return for customary payments or support.

The American missionary William H. Wiser studied the system in Karimpur village of Uttar Pradesh and described it in 'The Hindu Jajmani System' (1936). The patron family receiving services is called the 'jajman', and the service-providing family is called the 'kamin' or 'praja'.
Features of the system were:
- hereditary relationships, passed from father to son;
- payment mainly in kind, such as grain at harvest, together with gifts at festivals and ceremonies;
- caste-based division of labour;
- a relationship of mutual obligation, but also of inequality.
Examples of service castes included barbers, washermen, potters, carpenters and blacksmiths.

Scholars differ in how they judge the system. Some saw it as a system of cooperation and security. Others, such as Harold Gould and Oscar Lewis, emphasized that it was exploitative and maintained the domination of landowning castes. The system has declined because of the cash economy, new occupations, education, migration and democratic politics.

sections.title: Demographic Profile
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: A demographic profile describes a population through features such as size, growth, age structure, sex composition, birth and death rates and distribution. It helps sociologists understand the relationship between population and social conditions.
Census 2011 recorded the following figures for India:
- population: 1,210.8 million;
- decadal growth rate: 17.7 per cent (2001-2011);
- sex ratio: 943 females per 1,000 males;
- child sex ratio (0-6 years): 919;
- literacy rate: 74.04 per cent (male 82.1, female 65.5);
- population density: 382 persons per square kilometre.
In Mizoram, Census 2011 recorded a population of about 10.97 lakh, a sex ratio of 976 and a literacy rate of 91.3 per cent.
Important demographic terms are:
- crude birth rate (births per 1,000 population per year);
- crude death rate;
- infant mortality rate (deaths of infants under one year per 1,000 live births);
- total fertility rate (the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime);
- life expectancy;
- dependency ratio.

According to the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21), India's total fertility rate fell to 2.0, which is below the replacement level of 2.1. India's young population creates a potential 'demographic dividend', but only if young people receive education, health care and jobs.

sections.title: Causes of Rapid Population Growth
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Rapid population growth may result from high birth rates combined with declining death rates, early marriage, limited awareness or access to family planning and social preferences concerning family size.
The theory of demographic transition explains that societies move through stages:
- high birth and death rates;
- high birth rates but falling death rates, which causes rapid growth;
- falling birth rates;
- low birth and death rates.
India experienced the second stage for much of the twentieth century, when improved health care, vaccination and famine control reduced deaths, while birth rates remained high.
Social causes of high birth rates include:
- universal and early marriage;
- preference for sons;
- high infant mortality, which encourages more births;
- illiteracy, especially among women;
- religious and traditional beliefs;
- children seen as economic support in old age;
- poverty.

Thomas Robert Malthus, in 'An Essay on the Principle of Population' (1798), argued that population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, so checks such as famine and disease are inevitable unless people practise 'moral restraint'. Later scholars criticized Malthus for underestimating technological progress.

sections.title: Effects of Rapid Population Growth
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Rapid growth can increase pressure on employment, housing, education, health services, land and natural resources. Its effects depend on the capacity of the economy and institutions to provide opportunities and services.
Rapid population growth has several effects:
- Economic: unemployment, low per capita income, low savings and investment, and pressure on agricultural land.
- Social: overcrowding, urban slums, a shortage of schools and hospitals, and malnutrition.
- Environmental: deforestation, water scarcity and pollution.
Rapid growth can also increase competition for limited resources and contribute to social tensions, migration and crime.

However, some scholars argue that a large, young population can be an asset if it is educated and employed. The real problem is often not just numbers but the lack of development and fair distribution.

sections.title: Measures to Control Overpopulation
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Measures include education, public health, access to family planning, women's empowerment, delayed marriage and informed reproductive choices. Population policy works best when linked with social and economic development.

India became one of the first countries to launch an official family planning programme, in 1952. Later policy shifted from targets to a broader approach. The National Population Policy, 2000, aimed to bring the total fertility rate to replacement level and to stabilize the population, with a focus on reproductive health, child survival, girls' education and the minimum age at marriage.
The coercive sterilization drive during the Emergency (1975-77) produced strong public resentment and showed that population control must respect individual rights and consent.
Measures include:
- raising the age at marriage (the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, fixes 18 for girls and 21 for boys);
- female literacy;
- reducing infant mortality;
- providing contraceptive choices;
- incentives for small families;
- awareness through the media;
- schemes such as Mission Parivar Vikas, launched in 2016 for high-fertility districts.

sections.title: Scheduled Castes
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Scheduled Castes are communities recognized under the Constitution for special safeguards because of historical discrimination and social disadvantage. Constitutional measures seek equality, protection from discrimination and opportunities in education, employment and political representation.

Census 2011 recorded about 20.1 crore Scheduled Caste people, about 16.6 per cent of India's population. Castes are notified as Scheduled Castes by the President under Article 341, and Parliament can modify the list.
Important constitutional provisions are:
- Article 15(4), which allows special provisions for advancement;
- Article 16(4), which allows reservation in public employment;
- Article 17, which abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence;
- Article 46, which promotes their educational and economic interests;
- Articles 330 and 332, which reserve seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies;
- Article 338, which provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes.

Laws include the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act), and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. B.R. Ambedkar, the chief architect of the Constitution, led the movement for the rights and dignity of these communities.

sections.title: Scheduled Tribes
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Scheduled Tribes are constitutionally recognized tribal communities for whom special safeguards and development measures are provided. Policies address representation, education, welfare, land and protection of social and cultural interests.
Tribes are notified as Scheduled Tribes by the President under Article 342. The Lokur Committee (1965) gave criteria for identifying them:
- primitive traits;
- distinctive culture;
- geographical isolation;
- shyness of contact with the community at large;
- backwardness.
Constitutional safeguards include:
- Article 244 with the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas) and the Sixth Schedule (Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram);
- Article 275(1) grants;
- Article 338A, which provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (created by the 89th Amendment, 2003);
- reservation in legislatures and services.

Mizoram has three Autonomous District Councils under the Sixth Schedule: the Lai, Mara and Chakma councils. Important laws for tribal rights include the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA), and the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006.

sections.title: Other Backward Classes
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Other Backward Classes are socially and educationally backward groups identified for measures intended to improve equality of opportunity, including reservation and welfare policies under the constitutional and legal framework.

Article 340 provides for a commission to investigate the conditions of backward classes. The First Backward Classes Commission, chaired by Kaka Kalelkar, reported in 1955. The Second Backward Classes Commission, chaired by B.P. Mandal (the Mandal Commission), reported in 1980 and recommended 27 per cent reservation for OBCs in central government jobs. This was implemented in 1990.

In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court upheld OBC reservation, fixed a general ceiling of 50 per cent on reservations and excluded the 'creamy layer' (the better-off sections) from its benefits.

The 102nd Constitutional Amendment (2018) gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes under Article 338B. The 103rd Amendment (2019) separately introduced up to 10 per cent reservation for economically weaker sections (EWS) among those not covered by other reservations.

sections.title: PVTG
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups are tribal communities identified as especially vulnerable in socio-economic and developmental terms. They receive focused attention within tribal development programmes.

The Dhebar Commission (1960-61) noted large inequalities among tribes. This led to the identification of 'Primitive Tribal Groups' during the Fifth Five Year Plan, and they were renamed Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) in 2006. There are 75 PVTGs in India.
The criteria for identifying PVTGs are:
- a pre-agricultural level of technology;
- a very low level of literacy;
- economic backwardness (a subsistence economy);
- a stagnant or declining population.

Examples include the Jarawa, Onge, Sentinelese, Great Andamanese and Shompen of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, the Toda and Kurumba of Tamil Nadu, the Baiga of Madhya Pradesh, and the Reang (Bru) of Tripura. The Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN), launched in 2023, aims to provide housing, roads, water, health and education to PVTG habitations.

sections.title: Constitutional Provisions for Weaker Sections
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text: The Constitution provides equality before law, prohibits discrimination and permits special measures for disadvantaged groups. It also contains provisions relating to representation, educational and economic interests and safeguards for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
The Constitution provides the following safeguards:

- Fundamental Rights: Article 14 (equality before law), Article 15 (no discrimination), Article 16 (equality in public employment), Article 17 (abolition of untouchability), Article 23 (prohibition of forced labour) and Article 29 (protection of cultural interests);
- Directive Principles: Article 46 (promotion of the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and other weaker sections and their protection from social injustice and exploitation);
- political safeguards: reserved seats in the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and local bodies under the 73rd and 74th Amendments;
- administrative safeguards: national commissions, Scheduled Areas and the Tribal Advisory Council.
Development measures include:
- scholarships;
- hostels;
- Eklavya Model Residential Schools for tribal students;
- the Scheduled Caste Sub-Plan and Tribal Sub-Plan (now Development Action Plans);
- Stand-Up India loans;
- dedicated ministries, such as the Ministry of Tribal Affairs (1999) and the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

sections.title: Diversity, Unity and National Integration in Indian Society
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text:
Indian society is characterized by extensive diversity. People differ in language, religion, caste, tribe, ethnicity, region and cultural practices. This diversity is the result of a long history of migration, interaction and cultural development.

At the same time, Indian society contains important forces of unity. Historical interaction, economic interdependence, democratic institutions, the Constitution, education and communication connect people across regional and cultural boundaries. Multiculturalism provides a way of understanding how different communities may retain cultural identities while participating in a common society.

National integration does not require the disappearance of diversity. It refers to the growth of common belonging, political loyalty and cooperation among citizens. Constitutional values, democratic participation, equal citizenship and respect for cultural differences are therefore important for maintaining unity in a diverse society.
Many historical forces created India's diversity:
- migrations of different peoples;
- the arrival of religions such as Islam and Christianity, along with the growth of indigenous religions such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism;
- different geographical regions;
- different political histories.
These forces produced a pluralistic society. The Constitution's motto 'unity in diversity' expresses the idea that differences can coexist within a shared national identity.

Sociologists distinguish between integration and assimilation. Assimilation would mean the disappearance of minority cultures into a dominant culture. Integration means unity while preserving distinct identities. India's federal structure, linguistic reorganization of states (from 1956), and special provisions for the North-East (such as Article 371G for Mizoram and the Sixth Schedule) show an integrationist approach.
Threats to unity include:
- communal riots;
- caste-based violence;
- regional and ethnic conflicts;
- insurgency;
- economic disparity between regions;
- fake news spread through social media.
These challenges call for inclusive development, constitutional values, education and dialogue.
In conclusion, unity and diversity are not opposites. India's strength lies in its ability to accommodate differences within a democratic and constitutional framework.

sections.title: Segments of Indian Society: Tribal, Agrarian and Industrial
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text:
Indian society contains tribal, agrarian and industrial segments, each with distinctive forms of social organization. Tribal communities possess diverse cultural traditions, kinship systems and relationships with territory and natural resources. Agrarian society is organized around agriculture, land relations and rural institutions. Caste and class have historically influenced the distribution of land, occupations and status.

Industrial society develops through factory production, wage labour, urbanization and occupational specialization. Industrialization encourages migration and creates new forms of class and employment relations.

The village community has been a major setting of agrarian life. Traditional relations of service and exchange were sometimes organized through the Jajmani system, in which hereditary service groups and patron families were linked through customary obligations. Modern markets, education, state programmes, migration and technology have changed these older arrangements.

Sociologists sometimes describe Indian society as a 'plural society' with three main segments: tribal, agrarian (rural) and industrial (urban). They are connected to one another, and many people move between them through migration and changing occupations.
Tribal society is generally characterized by:
- territorial identity;
- clan and kinship organization;
- community ownership of land in some areas;
- shifting cultivation (jhum) in the hills of the North-East;
- their own customary laws.

Agrarian society has traditionally been organized around caste, land ownership, the jajmani system and village panchayats. Industrial society is associated with the factory system, cities, class, trade unions and secular, individualistic values.

The three segments are changing rapidly. Tribal areas are becoming integrated into markets and the state. Villages are affected by urban influences, and the Green Revolution and new technologies have transformed agriculture. Industrial cities depend on rural migrants. The boundaries between the segments are therefore becoming blurred.

In Mizoram, the traditional jhum economy is gradually giving way to settled cultivation, horticulture, government employment and business. Aizawl's urban population has grown rapidly, which shows the movement from tribal-agrarian life towards urban-industrial patterns.

sections.title: Population Dynamics in India
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text:
Population dynamics concerns the size, composition, distribution and change of population. A demographic profile uses indicators such as population growth, age, sex composition, fertility and mortality.

Rapid population growth can occur when birth rates remain high while death rates decline. Social practices, early marriage, limited family-planning access and preferences regarding family size may also influence growth. Rapid growth can place pressure on employment, housing, education, health care, land and public services.

Measures relating to population should therefore include education, better health care, women's empowerment, delayed marriage, family-planning services and informed reproductive choice. Population issues are closely connected with development and cannot be treated only as a question of numbers.
India is the world's most populous country, having overtaken China in 2023 according to United Nations estimates. Its population grew from about 36 crore in 1951 to about 121 crore in 2011.
Phases of growth:
- 1901-1921: stagnant population, with high birth and death rates and epidemics such as the 1918 influenza;
- 1921-1951: steady growth;
- 1951-1981: rapid, explosive growth as death rates fell;
- after 1981: high but gradually slowing growth.
The year 1921 is called the 'year of the great divide' because population has grown continuously since then.
Important features of India's population include:

- an adverse sex ratio, linked to son preference and sex-selective abortion and addressed by the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994, and the Beti Bachao Beti Padhao scheme (2015);
- a young age structure;
- growing urbanization (31.1 per cent urban in 2011);
- large regional differences, as between Kerala and Bihar.

Population policy has moved from a narrow focus on numbers towards a rights-based and development-based approach. The phrase 'development is the best contraceptive', associated with the 1974 World Population Conference at Bucharest, expresses this view.

sections.title: Weaker Sections and Constitutional Safeguards
context: SOC/MJ/200 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – I

blocks.text:
Indian society contains groups that have experienced historical social and economic disadvantages. The syllabus identifies Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes and Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups as important weaker sections for sociological study.

Scheduled Castes have historically faced severe caste discrimination. Scheduled Tribes include constitutionally recognized tribal communities with diverse social and cultural conditions. OBCs are groups identified as socially and educationally backward, while PVTGs are tribal groups considered particularly vulnerable.

The Constitution establishes equality and non-discrimination while also allowing special measures for disadvantaged groups. Safeguards include measures in education, public employment, political representation and welfare, along with protection of the interests of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. These provisions seek substantive equality and greater participation in social and political life.

The term 'weaker sections' refers to groups that suffer social, economic and educational disadvantages. Besides SCs, STs, OBCs and PVTGs, women, children, minorities, persons with disabilities and the elderly are often included.

Scheduled Castes suffered from untouchability, which denied them access to temples, wells, schools and dignified occupations. Social reformers such as Jyotirao Phule, Narayana Guru, Periyar, Mahatma Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar worked against untouchability. Ambedkar organized movements such as the Mahad Satyagraha (1927) for access to public water.

Reservation is often called 'protective discrimination' or 'compensatory discrimination'. Supporters see it as necessary for substantive equality. Critics raise issues such as merit, the creamy layer and the benefits reaching only a section of each group. Courts have tried to balance these concerns.

Atrocities, landlessness, low representation in higher positions and discrimination in the private sector remain serious problems. Strong implementation of laws, education, land reforms and economic empowerment are needed alongside reservation.

A social problem is a condition or pattern of behaviour considered harmful to a significant number of people and requiring collective attention. It is social because its causes and consequences are connected with social relationships and institutions.

Richard C. Fuller and Richard R. Myers (1941) defined a social problem as 'a condition which is defined by a considerable number of persons as a deviation from some social norm which they cherish'. Paul B. Horton and Gerald R. Leslie defined it as 'a condition affecting a significant number of people in ways considered undesirable, about which it is felt something can be done through collective social action'.

Two elements are important: an objective element (the actual harmful condition) and a subjective element (people's perception that it is a problem). Some conditions existed for a long time but were recognized as problems only later, such as domestic violence or child labour.
Social problems can be studied at the individual, family, community and national levels.

Social problems affect individuals as well as the wider community, are socially recognized as undesirable, arise from multiple causes and usually require organized social action. Their meaning can also vary across societies and historical periods.
Characteristics of social problems:
- They have social origins.
- They affect a large number of people.
- They are interrelated, for example poverty, illiteracy and unemployment.
- Different groups see them differently.
- They are relative to time and place.
- They require collective action.

What is considered a problem in one society may be accepted in another. For example, child marriage was once widely accepted in India but is now recognized as a serious social problem and is prohibited by law.
Social problems are also dynamic. New problems emerge with social change, such as cybercrime, online harassment, mobile phone addiction and environmental degradation.

Causes may include poverty, inequality, rapid social change, unemployment, discrimination, weak institutions, harmful customs, family disruption and failures of governance. Most social problems result from several interacting causes.
Sociologists group the causes of social problems into four types:
- economic causes (poverty, unemployment, inequality);
- social causes (family breakdown, caste discrimination, rapid urbanization);
- cultural causes (cultural lag, conflict of values, harmful traditions such as dowry);
- political causes (weak governance, corruption).

Durkheim's concept of anomie, Ogburn's cultural lag, Merton's strain theory (the gap between cultural goals and institutional means) and the idea of social disorganization all help explain the causes of social problems.
Psychological and biological factors may play a role in some cases, but sociologists stress the social environment, because the same condition affects groups in patterned ways.

Sociological approaches explain social problems from different viewpoints. Functional approaches examine disruption and institutional imbalance; conflict approaches emphasize inequality and power; interactionist approaches study social meanings, definitions and labelling.
Main approaches to studying social problems:
- The social pathology approach compared society to an organism and saw problems as diseases.
- The social disorganization approach, of the Chicago School, linked problems to the breakdown of norms.
- The value conflict approach, of Fuller and Myers, held that problems arise when groups hold conflicting values.
- The deviant behaviour approach, associated with Merton, studies behaviour that departs from norms.
- The labelling approach, of Howard Becker's 'Outsiders' (1963), argues that deviance is created when society labels certain acts and people as deviant.

Robert Merton's anomie theory identified five ways people adapt to the gap between goals and means: conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism and rebellion. For example, drug addicts were described as 'retreatists' who reject both goals and means.

The conflict approach, inspired by Marx, sees social problems as products of class inequality and capitalism. The feminist approach highlights patriarchy as a cause of problems such as domestic violence and harassment.

Domestic violence refers to abuse within domestic or intimate relationships. It may be physical, emotional, sexual or economic. It is connected with unequal power, harmful social attitudes and other social and economic factors.
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, defines domestic violence widely to include physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse. It provides:
- Protection Officers;
- protection orders;
- residence orders, so that a woman cannot be thrown out of the shared household;
- monetary relief;
- custody orders.

Cruelty by a husband or his relatives was punishable under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, now carried forward in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Dowry demands are prohibited under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
Causes include:
- patriarchal attitudes;
- dowry;
- alcoholism;
- economic dependence of women;
- social stigma that discourages reporting;
- the belief that family matters are private.
Help is available through the Women Helpline (181), One Stop Centres (Sakhi) and women's organisations.

Workplace harassment includes unwelcome behaviour that violates dignity and creates an unsafe or hostile working environment. Sexual harassment is a serious form of gender-based discrimination and requires institutional prevention and redress.

In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), the Supreme Court laid down guidelines to prevent sexual harassment at the workplace. The case arose after the gang rape of Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan. These guidelines were later replaced by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, commonly called the POSH Act.

The Act requires every employer with ten or more employees to set up an Internal Committee. Each district must have a Local Committee for smaller workplaces and the unorganized sector. The Act defines sexual harassment to include:
- unwelcome physical contact;
- demands for sexual favours;
- sexually coloured remarks;
- showing pornography;
- any other unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature.
Workplace harassment discourages women's participation in the workforce and violates their rights to equality, dignity and livelihood under Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21.

Child abuse includes physical, emotional or sexual abuse and neglect of children. It can cause serious harm to health, development, education and emotional well-being. Family, community and legal institutions have important protective roles.

The World Health Organization identifies four main types of child maltreatment: physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional abuse and neglect. Child labour, child marriage, child trafficking and corporal punishment are related problems.
The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, provides for child-friendly procedures, special courts and stronger punishments. Other laws include:
- the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015;
- the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, as amended in 2016;
- the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, which also prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment in schools.
The Childline service (1098) offers emergency help. The Integrated Child Protection Scheme, now part of Mission Vatsalya, supports Child Welfare Committees and child care institutions.

A juvenile in conflict with law is a child alleged or found to have committed an offence under the applicable juvenile justice framework. Sociology examines family conditions, peer influence, deprivation and social environment along with individual behaviour.

Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, a 'child in conflict with law' is a child below eighteen years of age who is alleged or found to have committed an offence. Such cases are handled by Juvenile Justice Boards, not by ordinary criminal courts.

After the Delhi gang rape case of 2012, the 2015 Act provided that children aged 16 to 18 accused of 'heinous offences' may, after a preliminary assessment by the Board, be tried as adults in a Children's Court.

The Act emphasizes reformation and rehabilitation rather than punishment. It provides for observation homes, special homes, counselling, community service and education. Sociological explanations of juvenile delinquency include:
- broken homes;
- poverty;
- peer pressure;
- the influence of the media;
- substance abuse;
- Edwin Sutherland's theory of differential association, which holds that criminal behaviour is learned through interaction with others.

Poverty refers to serious lack of resources needed for an acceptable standard of living. It affects nutrition, health, education, housing and opportunities and is closely connected with inequality and social exclusion.
Absolute poverty means lacking the minimum resources needed for survival, such as food, shelter and clothing. Relative poverty means having much less than the average standard of living in a society.

Poverty lines in India were estimated by expert committees such as the Tendulkar Committee (2009) and the Rangarajan Committee (2014). Based on the Tendulkar method, poverty in 2011-12 was estimated at about 21.9 per cent. NITI Aayog's National Multidimensional Poverty Index measures deprivation in health, education and standard of living.

Amartya Sen's capability approach defines poverty as a lack of the freedom and capabilities to live a life one values. Oscar Lewis's 'culture of poverty' thesis argued that poor people develop a way of life that passes poverty to the next generation, though critics say this blames the poor.
Anti-poverty programmes include:
- the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, which guarantees 100 days of wage employment to rural households;
- the National Food Security Act, 2013;
- the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana;
- the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission.
Corruption is the misuse of entrusted power or public position for private benefit. It weakens institutions, distorts distribution of resources and reduces public trust.
Forms of corruption include:
- bribery;
- nepotism (favouring relatives);
- embezzlement;
- extortion;
- favouritism in appointments;
- electoral corruption;
- corruption in public procurement.
Corruption may be petty (everyday bribes) or grand (large scams involving high officials).
Measures against corruption in India include:
- the Santhanam Committee (1962-64), which led to the Central Vigilance Commission;
- the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (amended in 2018);
- the Right to Information Act, 2005;
- the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013;
- e-governance;
- direct benefit transfer, which reduces leakages.

Sociologically, corruption is linked to weak institutions, the gap between salaries and expectations, patron-client relations, and social tolerance of corrupt practices. Ethical education and public vigilance are as important as laws.
Unemployment occurs when persons willing and able to work cannot obtain suitable employment. It has economic as well as social consequences, including insecurity, dependency and frustration.
Types of unemployment:
- open unemployment;
- disguised unemployment (more people working on a farm than necessary, so that some add nothing to output);
- seasonal unemployment (in agriculture between seasons);
- structural unemployment (due to a mismatch of skills and jobs);
- frictional unemployment (between jobs);
- educated unemployment;
- underemployment.
Unemployment data in India are collected through the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), run by the National Statistical Office.
- rapid growth of the labour force;
- slow job creation;
- an education system not linked to skills;
- preference for government jobs;
- dependence on agriculture;
- low industrial development in some regions.
In Mizoram and other north-eastern states, the dependence on limited government jobs makes educated unemployment a serious concern.
- skill development (Skill India, Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana);
- entrepreneurship schemes (Startup India, MUDRA loans);
- MGNREGA;
- developing tourism, horticulture and food processing.

Bonded labour is a form of forced labour linked to debt or obligation in which a person's freedom to leave employment is severely restricted. It is associated with exploitation, poverty and unequal social relations.

Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits 'begar' (forced labour without payment) and other forms of forced labour. The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, abolished bonded labour, cancelled bonded debts and provided for the release and rehabilitation of bonded labourers.

In Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984), the Supreme Court held that bonded labour violates the right to live with dignity under Article 21, and it directed the state to identify, release and rehabilitate bonded labourers.
Bonded labour is still found in brick kilns, stone quarries, agriculture, carpet weaving and domestic work, often among Dalit, tribal and migrant workers. Causes include:
- illiteracy;
- landlessness;
- caste-based inequality;
- weak enforcement.
The Central Sector Scheme for Rehabilitation of Bonded Labourer (2016) provides financial assistance to released labourers.

Drug addiction or dependence involves compulsive substance use despite harmful consequences. It affects individuals, families and communities and is influenced by psychological, social and economic conditions.

The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985, regulates and controls narcotic drugs. It provides strong punishments for trafficking, as well as treatment and de-addiction for users. The Narcotics Control Bureau coordinates drug law enforcement.

Mizoram and Manipur are affected by drug trafficking because of their proximity to the 'Golden Triangle', the region where Myanmar, Laos and Thailand meet, which is known for opium and heroin production. Heroin and methamphetamine are among the drugs seized in Mizoram.
Causes of drug addiction include:
- curiosity;
- stress;
- family problems;
- unemployment;
- availability of drugs.

The YMA, churches, NGOs and government de-addiction centres work on prevention and rehabilitation. The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, launched in 2020, is a national awareness campaign against substance abuse.

Alcoholism refers to harmful or dependent use of alcohol that interferes with health, family life, work and social responsibilities. Prevention requires awareness, treatment, family support and wider social measures.
Article 47 of the Constitution directs the state to work towards the prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs that are injurious to health, except for medicinal purposes.
Mizoram's policy on alcohol has changed several times:
- The Mizoram Liquor Total Prohibition Act, 1995, introduced total prohibition.
- This was relaxed by a 2014 law that allowed regulated sale from 2015.
- The Mizoram Liquor (Prohibition) Act, 2019, reintroduced prohibition.
This history shows the debate between prohibition and regulation.
Effects of alcoholism include:
- liver disease;
- road accidents;
- domestic violence;
- loss of work days;
- family breakdown;
- crime.
Treatment includes de-addiction centres, counselling, family therapy and self-help groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous.

HIV attacks the immune system and, without effective treatment, may progress to AIDS. As a social issue, HIV/AIDS also involves awareness, stigma, discrimination, access to health services and protection of affected persons.

The National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO), set up in 1992, implements the National AIDS Control Programme. The HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017, prohibits discrimination against people living with HIV in employment, education, health care and housing, and protects confidentiality.
HIV is transmitted through:
- unprotected sexual contact;
- sharing of infected needles;
- infected blood transfusion;
- transmission from mother to child.
It is not spread by casual contact such as shaking hands or sharing food. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) allows people with HIV to live long and healthy lives.

Mizoram has recorded the highest adult HIV prevalence among Indian states in recent national estimates. This is linked mainly to injecting drug use and unprotected sex. The Mizoram State AIDS Control Society, churches and NGOs run awareness, testing and treatment programmes. Reducing stigma is a key social task.

Human trafficking involves recruitment, transportation or control of persons for exploitation. Exploitation may include forced labour and sexual exploitation. Poverty, vulnerability, deception and organized criminal networks can contribute to trafficking.
The United Nations Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons (the Palermo Protocol, 2000) defines trafficking in terms of three elements:
- the act (recruitment, transport, harbouring);
- the means (threat, force, deception, abuse of vulnerability);
- the purpose (exploitation).

In India, trafficking is prohibited by Article 23 of the Constitution. It is addressed by the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, and by the trafficking provisions of the criminal law (the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, replaced the IPC). Anti-Human Trafficking Units operate in districts across the country.
Forms of trafficking include:
- sexual exploitation;
- forced labour;
- domestic servitude;
- forced marriage;
- child begging;
- organ trade.
Women and children from poor rural and border areas, including parts of the North-East, are vulnerable to traffickers who promise jobs or marriage in cities.

sections.title: Concept, Characteristics, Causes and Approaches to Social Problems

blocks.text:
A social problem is a social condition or pattern of behaviour widely regarded as undesirable and requiring collective action. Social problems are not simply private difficulties because they affect groups, institutions and social relationships.

They are characterized by social recognition, harmful consequences and multiple causes. Poverty, inequality, discrimination, rapid social change, unemployment, harmful customs and institutional weakness may contribute to different problems.

Sociology uses different theoretical approaches. Functional perspectives examine how institutional breakdown or imbalance produces problems. Conflict perspectives focus on inequality, competing interests and power. Interactionist approaches examine how behaviour is defined, interpreted and labelled. These approaches show that social problems must be understood within their wider social context.

C. Wright Mills distinguished between 'personal troubles' and 'public issues'. A social problem becomes a public issue when it affects many people and is linked to social structures. For example, one person losing a job is a personal trouble, but mass unemployment is a public issue.
Social problems pass through stages:
- awareness;
- policy determination;
- reform (Fuller and Myers's natural history of social problems).
The constructionist approach of Spector and Kitsuse emphasizes that social problems are 'claims-making activities' by groups who define a condition as problematic.

Merton and Nisbet, in 'Contemporary Social Problems', distinguished between 'social disorganization' (when the social system does not function well) and 'deviant behaviour' (when people depart from norms). Merton also distinguished between manifest problems, which are recognized, and latent problems, which exist but are not yet recognized.

Solutions require a combination of legal measures, welfare programmes, education, awareness, community participation and changes in social values. Sociological research helps in understanding causes and in planning effective solutions.

Domestic violence, workplace harassment, child abuse and juveniles in conflict with law are important social problems identified in the syllabus. Domestic violence involves abuse within family or intimate relationships and may take physical, emotional, sexual or economic forms. Workplace harassment violates dignity and equality and can prevent women from participating safely in employment.

Child abuse includes violence, exploitation and neglect that damage a child's development. Children also sometimes come into conflict with law. Sociological analysis considers family conditions, peer relations, deprivation and community environment rather than viewing juvenile behaviour in isolation.

These problems require legal protection, effective institutions, education, awareness, social support and changes in attitudes that normalize violence or inequality.

Data from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) show that 'cruelty by husband or his relatives' is among the most frequently registered crimes against women in India. However, many cases go unreported because of fear, stigma and dependence.

Feminist sociologists explain violence against women in terms of patriarchy, which is a system of male domination maintained through family, culture, economy and the state. Gender socialization that teaches boys to be dominant and girls to be submissive contributes to such violence.

Children are vulnerable because of their dependence on adults. Child abuse often occurs within the family or by known persons, which makes it harder to detect. Child protection requires awareness among parents and teachers, safe schools, child-friendly police and courts, and community vigilance.

Juvenile justice in India is based on the principle that children in conflict with law are themselves often victims of neglect, poverty or abuse, and that rehabilitation is more effective than punishment.
Important laws to remember:
- the PWDVA, 2005;
- the POSH Act, 2013;
- the POCSO Act, 2012;
- the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015;
- the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961;
- the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006.

sections.title: Poverty, Corruption, Unemployment and Bonded Labour

blocks.text:
Poverty is a condition of serious deprivation that limits access to food, housing, health, education and opportunities. Unemployment adds to economic insecurity and can produce dependency and social frustration.

Corruption is misuse of entrusted authority for private gain. It can divert public resources, weaken administration and reduce confidence in institutions. Bonded labour represents an extreme form of exploitation in which debt or obligation restricts a worker's freedom.

These problems are interconnected. Poverty and unemployment may increase vulnerability to exploitation, while corruption can weaken welfare and enforcement. Solutions therefore require employment opportunities, social protection, education, fair administration and effective enforcement of law.

Poverty, unemployment, corruption and bonded labour form a 'vicious circle'. Poor people have limited education and skills, which limits employment and keeps them poor. Indebtedness may lead to bonded labour. Corruption means that welfare benefits may not reach them.
Sociological perspectives:
- Functionalists such as Davis and Moore argued that inequality serves to place the most qualified people in important positions.
- Conflict theorists see poverty as the result of exploitation and unequal distribution of power and wealth.
- Interactionists study how poverty and unemployment affect identity, self-esteem and family relations.

India has reduced the proportion of people living in extreme poverty since 1991. However, inequality, informal employment, rural distress and regional disparities remain challenges. Government schemes, the RTI Act, social audits under MGNREGA, and the Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile (JAM) trinity for direct benefit transfer have aimed to improve delivery and reduce corruption.
Long-term solutions include:
- quality education;
- health care;
- skill development;
- land reforms;
- strong labour laws;
- transparent administration;
- active civil society.

sections.title: Drug Addiction, Alcoholism, HIV/AIDS and Human Trafficking

blocks.text:
Drug addiction and alcoholism affect health, family relationships, employment and community life. Their causes may include peer influence, availability of substances, stress, social environment and economic conditions. Prevention requires awareness, treatment and rehabilitation rather than relying only on punishment.

HIV/AIDS is both a health and social issue. Stigma and discrimination can prevent people from seeking testing and treatment. Accurate information, health services and social acceptance are important.

Human trafficking involves exploitation through recruitment, movement or control of vulnerable persons. Poverty, deception, lack of opportunities and criminal networks can increase vulnerability. Prevention requires protection of vulnerable groups, effective law enforcement, rehabilitation and public awareness.

These four problems are often linked. Injecting drug use can spread HIV. Alcoholism can lead to domestic violence and poverty. Traffickers may exploit people who are addicted or poor. In Mizoram, the link between drug use and HIV has been an important public health concern.
Prevention involves three levels:
- primary prevention, which stops problems before they start through awareness, education, sports and youth programmes;
- secondary prevention, which means early identification and counselling;
- tertiary prevention, which covers treatment, rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

Laws such as the NDPS Act, 1985, the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017, and the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, form the legal framework. Community-based organizations, churches and the YMA in Mizoram play an important role in prevention and rehabilitation.

Sociologists stress that these problems should be approached with compassion and evidence-based policies. Stigma and harsh punishment of users often drive problems underground, while support and treatment help people recover.
Socialization is the process through which individuals learn the norms, values, roles and ways of life of society and become participating social members.

Classic definitions: Ogburn said socialization is 'the process by which the individual learns to conform to the norms of the group'; Horton and Hunt described it as the process by which one internalizes the norms of one's groups so that a distinct self emerges, unique to the individual.
Socialization has two sides: from society's point of view, it transmits culture and maintains order; from the individual's point of view, it develops personality and a sense of self.
Cases of children reared in isolation, such as Anna and Isabelle studied by Kingsley Davis, show that without socialization a human being cannot develop normal speech and social behaviour.

Primary socialization occurs mainly in early childhood. Secondary socialization takes place in later institutions. Anticipatory socialization prepares a person for expected future roles, while re-socialization involves learning new patterns after earlier ones are replaced.

Examples: learning to speak, eat and dress at home (primary); learning rules and discipline at school or office (secondary); a trainee teacher practising teaching (anticipatory); and a person entering the army, a prison or a rehabilitation centre (re-socialization).
Erving Goffman's 'total institutions' (such as prisons and military camps) are settings of intense re-socialization where the old identity is stripped away and a new one is built.
Some textbooks also mention developmental socialization (building on earlier learning) and reverse socialization (the young teaching the old, for example about technology).

Socialization begins in childhood and continues through later stages of life. Family dominates early learning, while school, peers, work and other institutions become important as social roles expand.

George Herbert Mead described three stages in the development of the self: the preparatory (imitation) stage, the play stage (taking the role of specific others) and the game stage (understanding the 'generalized other').
Following Freud and Parsons, Indian textbooks often list the oral stage, the anal stage, the oedipal stage and adolescence as stages of childhood socialization.
Socialization continues in adulthood (marriage, work, parenthood) and old age (retirement, widowhood), showing that it is lifelong.
Major agents include family, school, peer groups, religion, media and other institutions. Each contributes to the learning of norms, values and expected behaviour.

The family teaches language, manners, religion and gender roles; the school teaches knowledge, discipline and citizenship; peer groups teach cooperation and equality and may introduce new values; religion teaches moral codes; and mass media and social media spread ideas and role models.
Other agents include the workplace, the state and law, sports teams and voluntary associations.
In Mizoram, the church, Sunday school, youth fellowships and the YMA are important agents that promote values such as tlawmngaihna and community service.
Internalization occurs when social norms and values become accepted as part of an individual's own outlook, so conformity is not based only on external pressure.
Freud explained internalization through the development of the superego, the part of personality that represents society's moral standards and acts as a conscience.
When norms are internalized, people feel guilt or shame when they break them, even if no one else knows. This is why internalization is the most effective form of social control.
Durkheim argued that moral education should help children internalize the values of society so that they feel attached to the group and respect its rules.

Culture supplies the language, values, beliefs, symbols and behavioural expectations that individuals learn through socialization. Different cultures therefore produce different patterns of social learning.
Culture decides what is taught and how it is taught. For example, some cultures emphasize individual achievement and independence, while others emphasize obedience, cooperation and family loyalty.

Margaret Mead's study 'Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies' (1935) in New Guinea suggested that gender behaviour differs across cultures, showing that much of what we consider 'masculine' or 'feminine' is learned through culture.

In Mizo culture, children traditionally learned values such as hospitality, courage, helpfulness and respect for elders through stories, songs, community work and, in the past, the zawlbuk (bachelors' dormitory).
Socialization develops personality, social identity, role performance and knowledge of accepted behaviour. It also transmits culture from one generation to another.

Socialization helps in the development of self and personality, the learning of language and skills, role learning, the formation of values, the regulation of behaviour and the transmission of culture.
It also prepares individuals for occupations and citizenship, and helps in adjusting to new situations through re-socialization.
Faulty socialization can lead to deviance, delinquency and personality problems, which shows its importance for both the individual and society.
Culture is the learned and shared way of life of a society, including values, beliefs, norms, language, knowledge, customs and material objects.
E.B. Tylor defined culture as 'that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society'.

Bronislaw Malinowski described culture as 'the handiwork of man and the medium through which he achieves his ends'. Robert Bierstedt defined it as 'the complex whole that consists of all the ways we think and do and everything we have as members of society'.
Culture is what distinguishes human beings from animals, since humans rely on learned behaviour rather than instinct.
Culture is learned, shared, transmitted, symbolic and adaptive. It provides continuity but also changes through innovation and contact.

Other characteristics include: culture is social, not individual; it satisfies human needs; it is integrated (its parts are connected); it is cumulative (it grows over time); and it varies from society to society.
Culture is symbolic because it depends on language and other symbols to carry meaning. Leslie White argued that symbolling is the basis of all human culture.
Culture is also normative: it provides standards for judging behaviour as right or wrong.
Culture is commonly distinguished into material culture, consisting of physical objects and technology, and non-material culture, consisting of values, beliefs, norms, language and ideas.

The distinction between material and non-material culture was made by W.F. Ogburn. Material culture includes houses, tools, machines, clothes and food; non-material culture includes ideas, beliefs, customs, values and language.
Other related types are subculture (the culture of a group within society, such as youth culture), counter-culture (which opposes dominant values), popular culture and high culture.
Examples from Mizoram: the 'puan', bamboo houses and traditional dance instruments are material culture; tlawmngaihna, the Mizo language and customary practices are non-material culture.
Cultural lag occurs when different parts of culture change at unequal speeds, especially when technology changes faster than laws, institutions or values.

W.F. Ogburn introduced the concept in 'Social Change' (1922). He argued that material culture changes faster because of inventions, while adaptive culture (customs, laws, beliefs) changes more slowly.

Examples: the spread of mobile phones and social media has been faster than the development of norms and laws on privacy, online safety and cybercrime; medical technology has raised ethical issues that law is still addressing.
Cultural lag can lead to social problems and disorganization during periods of rapid change.

sections.title: Socialization: Meaning, Types, Stages and Agents

blocks.text:
Socialization is the lifelong process through which individuals learn society's norms, values, roles and cultural expectations. It connects individual development with social life.

Primary socialization occurs mainly during childhood, especially within the family. Secondary socialization takes place in schools, peer groups, workplaces and other institutions. Anticipatory socialization prepares people for future roles, while re-socialization involves learning substantially new patterns of behaviour.

Family, school, peer groups, religion and media are major agents. Their relative influence changes through the life course. Through these agents, individuals learn language, discipline, identity and social responsibilities. Socialization is therefore essential both for personality development and for continuity of society.

Charles Horton Cooley's 'looking-glass self' explains that the self develops through three steps: we imagine how we appear to others, we imagine their judgement of us, and we develop feelings such as pride or shame as a result.

George Herbert Mead distinguished between the 'I' (the spontaneous, creative part of the self) and the 'me' (the social self formed by internalized expectations). The self develops through play and games in which the child learns to take the role of others.
Different agents dominate at different stages: the family in childhood, the school and peers in adolescence, and the workplace and media in adulthood.

Socialization can fail or be inadequate because of neglect, family conflict or harmful influences. Strong families, good schools and supportive communities are therefore essential for healthy socialization.

The process of socialization involves interaction, learning and internalization. Internalization occurs when social norms and values become part of a person's own understanding and guide behaviour from within.

Culture plays a central role because socialization always transmits a particular language, set of values, symbols and accepted practices. Since cultures differ, socialization patterns also differ between societies.

Socialization is important because it enables individuals to communicate, perform social roles and participate in institutions. It develops social identity and personality and transmits culture across generations. Without socialization, organized social life and cultural continuity would be difficult.
Socialization is not just learning but also the formation of identity. Through interaction, individuals come to see themselves as members of a family, community, religion and nation.
Sigmund Freud's model of personality (id, ego and superego) shows how society's demands, represented by the superego, control biological drives, represented by the id.
Jean Piaget's stages of cognitive development (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational) show that the way children learn depends on their age and mental development.
Socialization is a two-way process: individuals are shaped by society, but they also interpret, resist and change social norms. This is why each generation brings some change to culture.

sections.title: Culture: Meaning, Characteristics, Types and Cultural Lag

blocks.text:
Culture is the learned and shared way of life of a society. It includes language, beliefs, values, norms, customs, knowledge and material objects.

Culture is learned rather than biologically inherited. It is shared by members, transmitted between generations, expressed through symbols and capable of change. Material culture includes tools, technology and physical products, while non-material culture includes beliefs, values, norms and ideas.

Cultural lag occurs when different parts of culture change at different rates. Technology may change rapidly while law, institutions or values adjust more slowly. This gap can create temporary tension and adjustment problems. Culture therefore provides both continuity and a framework within which social change takes place.
Culture includes both 'ideal culture' (the values and norms people say they follow) and 'real culture' (what people actually do). The gap between them is common in every society.

Ethnocentrism is the tendency to judge other cultures by the standards of one's own, while cultural relativism tries to understand each culture in its own context. Culture shock is the confusion experienced when moving into a very different culture.
Cultural change occurs through discovery, invention and diffusion. Acculturation results from continuous contact between cultures, and assimilation is the fuller merging of cultures.

In conclusion, culture is the blueprint of social life; socialization is the process through which individuals learn it; and cultural lag reminds us that different parts of culture change at different speeds.

sections.title: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II
SHORT NOTES
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

sections.title: Joint Family
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: A joint family generally includes members of more than one generation who are linked by kinship and share important family obligations. Traditional joint families may involve common residence, property, authority and economic cooperation.

Iravati Karve defined the joint family as 'a group of people who generally live under one roof, who eat food cooked at one hearth, who hold property in common, who participate in common family worship and who are related to each other as some particular type of kindred'.

Two schools of Hindu law govern joint family property: Mitakshara (most of India), in which sons acquire a right in ancestral property by birth, and Dayabhaga (Bengal and Assam), in which property passes after the father's death.

I.P. Desai pointed out that jointness is a matter of degree, and he distinguished between residential (household) jointness and functional jointness, where members live separately but cooperate in property, rituals and obligations.

sections.title: Characteristics of Joint Family
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Important characteristics may include a relatively large kin group, common responsibilities, cooperation, shared property or economic interests and authority structured by age and kinship. Actual forms vary across regions and communities.

Characteristics of the joint family include large size, common residence, common kitchen, common property, common worship, authority of the eldest male (the 'karta'), cooperative economy, mutual obligations and subordination of individual interests to the family.

Advantages include social security for the old, the sick and the widowed, division of labour, economy of expenditure, preservation of property and culture, and socialization of children by many elders.
Disadvantages pointed out by critics include restriction of individual freedom, lower status of women, conflicts between members, and a tendency for some members to depend on others.

sections.title: Forces of Change in Joint Family
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Urbanization, migration, education, occupational mobility, housing conditions, individual aspirations and changing gender roles have influenced the joint family system.

Factors of change include industrialization and new occupations, urbanization and lack of space in cities, migration for education and work, Western education and individualistic values, and the changing status and employment of women.

Legislation has also played a role: the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955; the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and its 2005 amendment, which gave daughters equal coparcenary rights in joint family property; and the Special Marriage Act, 1954.
Mass media, new means of transport and communication, and the spread of a cash economy have also weakened the economic basis of the traditional joint family.

sections.title: Changing Family in India
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Family life in India has undergone changes in household size, authority, residence, gender roles and intergenerational relations. Nuclear households have increased in many settings, although wider kinship obligations often remain important.

Studies show that the nuclear household has grown, but the extended family remains important for ceremonies, economic help, child care and care of the elderly. A.M. Shah argued that the 'household' and the 'family' should be distinguished, since many families live in several households.
Changes include decline of the authority of elders, greater equality between spouses, more freedom for young people in education and marriage, and smaller families due to family planning.
New problems include the neglect of the elderly, addressed by the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, and the double burden on working women.

sections.title: Hindu Marriage
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Hindu marriage has historically been shaped by religious, kinship and caste traditions. Modern law and social change have influenced age at marriage, spouse selection, divorce, remarriage and rights within marriage.

K.M. Kapadia, in 'Marriage and Family in India', said that the aims of Hindu marriage are dharma (religious duty), praja (progeny) and rati (pleasure), with dharma being the most important. Hindu marriage was traditionally regarded as a sacrament (samskara), not a contract.

The ancient texts describe eight forms of Hindu marriage: Brahma, Daiva, Arsha and Prajapatya (approved forms), and Asura, Gandharva, Rakshasa and Paisacha (disapproved forms). Rituals such as kanyadan, panigrahana and saptapadi (seven steps around the sacred fire) are important.

The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, made Hindu marriage monogamous, fixed a minimum age, allowed divorce on specified grounds and permitted inter-caste marriage. Divorce by mutual consent was added in 1976.

sections.title: Muslim Marriage
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Muslim marriage is governed by religious and legal principles concerning marital agreement, rights and obligations. Social practices vary among communities and are also affected by modern law and social change.

Muslim marriage (nikah) is regarded as a civil contract. Its essential elements include a proposal (ijab) and acceptance (qubul), the consent of both parties, the presence of witnesses, and mahr (dower), which is a sum given by the husband to the wife as a mark of respect and security.

Types of marriage include sahih (valid), batil (void) and fasid (irregular); Shia law also recognizes muta, a temporary marriage. Islamic law permits a man up to four wives under conditions, though monogamy is common in practice.

Divorce may take forms such as talaq (by the husband), khula (initiated by the wife with return of mahr) and mubarat (by mutual consent). The Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939, gave women grounds for divorce. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court declared instant triple talaq unconstitutional, and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, made it void and a punishable offence.

sections.title: Christian Marriage
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Christian marriage is shaped by Christian religious traditions and applicable legal provisions. Family and church practices may influence ceremonies and marital expectations, while contemporary changes affect spouse selection and family roles.
Christian marriage is considered both a sacrament (especially in the Catholic Church) and a covenant between husband and wife before God. It is monogamous and is ideally lifelong.

The Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, governs the solemnization of Christian marriages in much of India, and the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 (amended in 2001), governs divorce. Rituals include engagement, publication of banns, a church ceremony, exchange of vows and rings, and blessing by the minister.

In Mizoram, almost all marriages are church weddings combining Christian rites with Mizo customs such as the bride price ('man'). The Mizo Marriage, Divorce and Inheritance of Property Act, 2014, provides the legal framework for marriage and divorce among the Mizo.

sections.title: Changing Marriage in India
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II
