blocks.text: Marriage in India is changing through education, urbanization, legal reform, employment and greater individual choice. Changes include spouse selection, age at marriage, gender expectations and attitudes to divorce and remarriage.

Changes include a rising age at marriage, decline of child marriage, more inter-caste and inter-religious marriages in cities, online matrimonial services, love-cum-arranged marriages, and greater acceptance of divorce and widow remarriage.

Laws such as the Special Marriage Act, 1954, the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, and the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, have shaped marriage practices. However, problems such as dowry deaths and honour killings still occur.
Marriage is gradually moving from being an alliance between families to being a partnership between individuals, though family approval remains important for most Indians.

sections.title: Features of Caste System
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: The caste system traditionally involved hereditary membership, hierarchy, restrictions on social interaction and marriage, and links between caste and occupation. Its form has varied historically and regionally.

G.S. Ghurye, in 'Caste and Race in India' (1932), listed six features of caste: segmental division of society; hierarchy; restrictions on feeding and social intercourse; civil and religious disabilities and privileges of different sections; lack of unrestricted choice of occupation; and restrictions on marriage (endogamy).
The varna system has four categories (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra), while jati refers to the thousands of local endogamous caste groups. Untouchables were placed outside the varna system.
Caste is based on birth and is closed, unlike class, which is more open and based on economic position.

sections.title: Perspectives on Caste
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Caste has been studied from structural, cultural, economic and political perspectives. Sociologists examine hierarchy, purity and pollution, occupation, power, class and changing caste identities.

The Indological or cultural perspective (G.S. Ghurye, Louis Dumont) studies caste through Hindu texts and ideas. Dumont, in 'Homo Hierarchicus' (1966), argued that the opposition between purity and impurity is the basic principle of the caste system.

The structural-functional perspective (M.N. Srinivas) studied caste in villages through fieldwork and developed concepts such as dominant caste, Sanskritization and vote bank. A dominant caste is numerically strong, economically and politically powerful, and has a high ritual status locally.

The conflict and subaltern perspectives (B.R. Ambedkar, Gail Omvedt, Kancha Ilaiah) see caste as a system of exploitation and graded inequality. Ambedkar's 'Annihilation of Caste' (1936) called for the destruction of the caste system. Andre Beteille, in 'Caste, Class and Power' (1965), studied the relationship between caste, class and political power in a Tamil Nadu village.

sections.title: Changes in Caste System
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Urbanization, education, democratic politics, law, occupational mobility and economic change have weakened some traditional restrictions while caste continues to influence identity, marriage and politics in many settings.

Changes include the decline of restrictions on food and social intercourse, the loosening of the link between caste and occupation, legal abolition of untouchability, reservation, and the rise of caste-based political mobilization.
Srinivas observed that caste has become more important in politics even as its ritual aspects decline. Rajni Kothari, in 'Caste in Indian Politics' (1970), discussed the 'politicization of caste'.

Caste persists in matrimony, in local power structures and sometimes in violence and discrimination. Dalit movements and organizations have challenged caste domination and demanded equality and dignity.

sections.title: Zonal Distribution of Tribes
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Tribal communities in India are distributed across several broad geographical zones, including the North-East, central and eastern regions, western areas and parts of southern India. These communities are highly diverse.

L.P. Vidyarthi and others have divided Indian tribes into zones: the North-Eastern zone (Mizo, Naga, Khasi, Garo, Bodo and others); the Central zone (Gond, Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Ho, Bhil in parts); the Western zone (Bhil, Meena, Warli); the Southern zone (Toda, Irula, Kurumba, Chenchu); and the Island zone (Andaman and Nicobar groups such as the Onge and Jarawa).

Some scholars also identify a Himalayan zone (Gaddi, Bhotia, Lepcha). The central Indian belt has the largest tribal population in absolute numbers, while the North-Eastern states have the highest proportion of tribal people.
Mizoram, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh have tribal majorities, and Lakshadweep also has a predominantly Scheduled Tribe population.

sections.title: Colonial Policies and Tribes
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Colonial rule altered tribal life through administrative control, forest and land policies, taxation and changes in local authority. Effects differed across regions and contributed to resistance as well as social transformation.

Colonial forest laws, such as the Indian Forest Acts of 1865 and 1878, declared large forest areas as government property and restricted tribal rights of shifting cultivation, hunting and collection of forest produce.

The colonial land revenue system introduced private ownership of land and brought moneylenders, traders and landlords into tribal areas, leading to land alienation and indebtedness. This contributed to revolts such as the Santhal Hul (1855-56) and the Munda Ulgulan led by Birsa Munda (1899-1900).

In the North-East, the British followed a policy of limited interference. The Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873, introduced the Inner Line, which still regulates entry into Mizoram through the Inner Line Permit. Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the Lushai Hills was declared an 'Excluded Area'.

sections.title: Integration and Autonomy
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Debates on tribal policy concern participation in wider national life while protecting cultural identity, land, institutions and self-governance. Integration and autonomy are therefore important issues in tribal sociology.

Three approaches have been debated: isolation, associated with Verrier Elwin's early view that tribes should be protected in a kind of 'national park'; assimilation, associated with G.S. Ghurye, who described tribes as 'backward Hindus' who should be absorbed into Hindu society; and integration, the policy adopted after independence.

Jawaharlal Nehru's 'Panchsheel' for tribal development (stated in his foreword to Elwin's 'A Philosophy for NEFA') included: people should develop along the lines of their own genius; tribal rights to land and forests should be respected; tribal people should be trained to run their own administration; tribal areas should not be over-administered; and results should be judged by the quality of human character rather than money spent.

Autonomy is provided through the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA (1996), the Forest Rights Act (2006), and special provisions such as Article 371G for Mizoram, which protects Mizo customary law and land ownership.

sections.title: Modern Factors of Tribal Transformation
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text: Education, markets, migration, Christianity and other religions, communication, state policy, urbanization and political mobilization have contributed to transformation among tribal communities.
Education has been a major force of change, especially in the North-East, where Christian missions introduced schools. Mizoram's high literacy is closely connected with missionary education.

Other factors include the spread of the market economy, improved roads and communication, government development programmes, reservation in jobs and education, urbanization, migration to cities for education and work, and political movements for identity and autonomy.

These changes have produced both opportunities (education, employment, political participation) and challenges (loss of traditional culture, land alienation in some regions, internal inequality among tribes, and identity conflicts).

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

sections.title: Joint Family and the Changing Family in India
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text:
The joint family has been an important institution in discussions of Indian society. It generally contains a wider kin group across generations and may involve common residence, property, economic cooperation and family authority.

The joint family has never been identical throughout India. Its form varies by region, class, caste and community. Modern changes such as urbanization, migration, education, salaried employment, limited urban housing and changing individual aspirations have affected household organization.

The growth of nuclear households does not necessarily mean that extended kinship has disappeared. Families living separately may continue to exchange economic help, care and participate in rituals. The changing family in India is therefore better understood as adaptation and reorganization rather than a simple replacement of one family form by another.
Henry Maine described the Indian joint family as a 'patriarchal' unit and thought it would disappear with modernization. Later sociologists showed that it adapted rather than disappeared.

I.P. Desai's study in Mahuva (Gujarat) found that most families had some jointness, even if they lived separately. K.M. Kapadia and others observed that nuclear households often maintain strong ties with the larger family.

Positive changes include greater freedom, equality for women and children, and more democratic decision-making. Negative effects include insecurity for the elderly and loss of traditional support systems.

In Mizoram, families are traditionally patrilineal and smaller than the classic Hindu joint family. The youngest son traditionally stayed with and cared for the parents, while other sons set up their own households. Today, urbanization and government employment have increased nuclear households, while clan and kin ties remain important.
In conclusion, the Indian family is best described as a 'changing but resilient' institution that combines traditional obligations with modern values.

sections.title: Marriage among Hindus, Muslims and Christians and Changing Marriage in India
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text:
Marriage in India is shaped by religious traditions, kinship rules, community customs and law. Hindu marriage has historically been connected with religious and caste practices. Muslim marriage is organized through Islamic principles and marital rights and obligations. Christian marriage is shaped by Christian religious traditions and applicable law.

There is considerable diversity within each religious community, so no single practice represents all members. Modern education, urbanization, legal reform, employment and communication have influenced marriage across communities.

Contemporary changes include increasing individual participation in spouse selection, changes in age at marriage, changing gender roles and new attitudes towards divorce and remarriage. Family involvement remains important in many marriages, showing the coexistence of continuity and change.

A comparison: Hindu marriage was traditionally a sacrament, indissoluble and linked with caste and gotra rules; Muslim marriage is a civil contract with mahr and the possibility of divorce; Christian marriage is a sacrament or covenant, monogamous and solemnized in church.

Personal laws governing marriage include the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (also applying to Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists), Muslim personal law, the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, 1939, the Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1872, the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936, and the Special Marriage Act, 1954, for inter-religious and civil marriages.

Article 44 of the Constitution directs the state to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout India. This remains a debated issue. Uttarakhand passed a Uniform Civil Code law in 2024.
Common trends across religions include rising age at marriage, decline of polygamy, greater individual choice, legal protection for women and the influence of education and urbanization.
In tribal societies such as the Mizo, marriage is governed by customary law and church practices, showing that India's diversity in marriage extends beyond the major religions.

sections.title: Caste System in India: Features, Perspectives and Change
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text:
Caste is a major institution in the sociological study of Indian society. Traditional caste organization involved hereditary membership, hierarchy, endogamy, occupational connections and restrictions on social interaction. Ideas of purity and pollution were important in some interpretations.

Different sociological perspectives emphasize different aspects. Structural and cultural approaches examine hierarchy and ritual status, while economic and political approaches examine land, class, power and mobilization.

The caste system has changed through education, urbanization, industrialization, constitutional law, democratic politics and occupational mobility. Traditional restrictions have weakened in many areas, yet caste continues to influence marriage, social identity, political organization and access to networks. Caste in contemporary India therefore shows both transformation and persistence.

Theories of the origin of caste include the traditional theory (divine origin from the 'Purusha Sukta' of the Rig Veda), the racial theory (H.H. Risley, who linked caste with race), the occupational theory (Nesfield), and the political theory (Brahmin domination). Most sociologists believe caste developed through a combination of factors over a long period.
M.N. Srinivas's concepts are important: Sanskritization explains mobility within the caste system; the 'dominant caste' explains village power; and 'vote bank' explains caste in electoral politics.

Factors of change include Western education, industrialization, urbanization, means of transport, legal reforms (abolition of untouchability, reservation), democratic politics, social reform movements and the Dalit movement.

Despite change, caste continues in new forms: caste associations, caste-based political parties, matrimonial preferences and caste-based violence. Andre Beteille noted that caste, class and power have become more separated in modern India, though they still overlap.

In conclusion, caste in contemporary India shows a paradox: its ritual basis is weakening, but its role in identity and politics continues. The constitutional vision is of a society based on equality and dignity for all.

sections.title: Tribal Situations in India
context: SOC/MJ/203 – SOCIOLOGY OF INDIAN SOCIETY – II

blocks.text:
India's tribal communities are highly diverse and are distributed across the North-East, central and eastern India, western regions and parts of the south. Their languages, social institutions, economies and histories differ greatly.

Colonial administration transformed many tribal regions through forest laws, land policies, taxation and new administrative structures. These interventions affected customary rights and sometimes generated resistance.

After independence, tribal policy has faced the challenge of combining development and integration with protection of cultural identity, land and autonomy. Modern transformation is influenced by education, markets, migration, communication, state programmes, religion, urbanization and political mobilization. Tribal change should therefore be understood in relation to both internal social processes and wider political and economic forces.
The Constitution does not define 'tribe', but Article 366(25) refers to Scheduled Tribes as communities specified under Article 342. Census 2011 counted about 10.4 crore Scheduled Tribe persons.

Tribal problems include land alienation, indebtedness, displacement due to dams, mines and industrial projects, low literacy in some regions, poor health and nutrition, loss of forest rights, and exploitation by outsiders. The Xaxa Committee (2014) studied the socio-economic, health and educational status of tribal communities.

Tribal movements have ranged from agrarian and forest-based struggles to political movements for autonomy and statehood, such as the movements that led to the creation of Mizoram (state in 1987), Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh (2000).

In Mizoram, the Mizo National Front movement and the 1986 Mizo Peace Accord led to statehood. Article 371G protects Mizo religious and social practices, customary law, administration of civil and criminal justice according to Mizo customary law, and ownership and transfer of land.
Tribal development requires respect for culture, participation of the people in planning, protection of land and forest rights, education in mother tongue, health care and sustainable livelihoods.
Social change refers to significant alteration in social relationships, institutions, values or structures over time. Change may be gradual or rapid and may affect one part or many parts of society.

MacIver and Page said social change refers to changes in social relationships. Kingsley Davis defined it as 'only such alterations as occur in social organization, that is, the structure and functions of society'. Morris Ginsberg described it as 'a change in social structure'.

Social change is distinct from cultural change, though they overlap. Kingsley Davis noted that cultural change is broader, including changes in art, science, technology and philosophy, while social change is a part of it.
Examples of social change in India include the decline of untouchability, changing status of women, growth of nuclear families and the spread of education.
Social change is universal, continuous and variable in speed and direction. It may be planned or unplanned and its effects are often uneven across groups and institutions.

Characteristics: social change is universal; it is a community change, not merely individual change; its speed differs across societies and periods; it is difficult to predict; it is often a chain reaction because a change in one part affects others; and it is value-neutral (neither good nor bad in itself).
Change may be planned (such as land reform, family planning and Panchayati Raj) or unplanned (such as the effects of natural disasters or technological diffusion).
The pace of change has increased greatly in modern times due to science, technology, communication and globalization.

Progress generally implies movement toward a condition considered better according to certain values. Development refers to broader processes of economic, social and institutional transformation. Not every social change is necessarily progress.

Progress is change in a desired direction, judged according to values. Since values differ, what is progress for one group may not be progress for another. MacIver said progress implies 'not merely direction but direction towards some final goal'.

Development has economic and social dimensions. Economic development refers to growth in income and production, while human development, as measured by the UNDP's Human Development Index (introduced in 1990), includes health, education and standard of living.

Amartya Sen's 'Development as Freedom' (1999) defines development as the expansion of people's real freedoms. Sustainable development, defined in the Brundtland Report (1987), means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Evolutionary change is gradual and cumulative, while revolutionary change is rapid and involves major transformation of institutions or power relations.

Evolution comes from the Latin 'evolvere' meaning 'to unfold'. Social evolution refers to a process of gradual change from simple to complex. Herbert Spencer applied Darwin's idea of evolution to society.

Revolution involves sudden, radical and often violent change in political, economic or social structure. Examples include the French Revolution (1789), the Russian Revolution (1917) and the Chinese Revolution (1949). The Industrial Revolution was a revolution in technology and economy, though it took place over decades.
Some scholars also discuss reform, which is planned, gradual and peaceful change within the existing system, such as social reform movements in India.
Obstacles may include rigid traditions, vested interests, inequality, resistance to innovation, lack of education or resources and institutions that benefit from existing arrangements.

Obstacles include: traditionalism and fear of the new; vested interests of groups who benefit from existing arrangements; ignorance and illiteracy; superstitions; caste, religious and kinship restrictions; economic constraints; geographical isolation; and the 'habit' of following customs.
Psychological factors such as fear of the unknown and resistance to new ideas are also important. Administrative obstacles include poor implementation and corruption.
Change agents such as education, mass media, social movements and leadership help to overcome these obstacles.

Technology changes production, communication, transport, occupations and everyday relationships. New technologies can transform institutions and create new social opportunities as well as new inequalities.

W.F. Ogburn is the main exponent of the technological theory of change; he argued that inventions in material culture are the main cause of social change, producing cultural lag. Karl Marx also emphasized technology when he wrote that 'the hand-mill gives you society with the feudal lord; the steam-mill, society with the industrial capitalist'.

Examples of technological change: the steam engine and factory system led to urbanization; the printing press spread literacy; the automobile and railways increased mobility; and the internet and smartphones have transformed communication, business, education and politics.

In India, initiatives such as Digital India (2015), Aadhaar, UPI payments and online education show how technology is transforming society, but the 'digital divide' between urban and rural, rich and poor also creates new inequalities.
Education spreads knowledge and skills, influences values and aspirations and can promote occupational and social mobility. It is an important agent of planned social change.

Education is regarded as the most important agent of planned social change. It changes attitudes, removes superstitions, creates awareness of rights, promotes mobility and prepares people for new occupations.

The Indian Constitution made free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 a fundamental right under Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002), implemented through the Right to Education Act, 2009. The National Education Policy, 2020, aims for universal access, multidisciplinary learning and skill development.
In Mizoram, mission education from the late nineteenth century led to rapid literacy and the emergence of an educated middle class, showing the transformative power of education.
Changes in values, beliefs, ideas and cultural contact can alter social behaviour and institutions. Cultural diffusion and new ideologies are important sources of change.
Max Weber showed in 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism' that religious ideas can promote social change, in contrast to Marx's emphasis on economic factors.

Cultural factors of change include new ideas and ideologies (such as democracy, nationalism, socialism and feminism), religious reform movements, cultural contact through migration and media, and changes in values about family, gender and individual rights.

In India, social reform movements such as the Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, and the work of reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Jyotirao Phule and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar challenged practices like sati, child marriage and caste discrimination.
Changes in production, markets, employment, property and income can transform class relations, family patterns, migration and social institutions.

Karl Marx is the main exponent of economic determinism. He argued that the economic base (the forces and relations of production) shapes the superstructure (law, politics, religion, family, culture). When the forces of production change, they come into conflict with existing relations of production, leading to social change.

Examples of economic change: industrialization creating a working class; the Green Revolution changing agrarian relations; liberalization since 1991 creating new middle classes and consumer culture; and the growth of the service sector and IT industry.
Economic factors interact with others, so many sociologists reject pure economic determinism but accept that economic change is a powerful force.
Evolutionary theories view social change as a gradual process through which societies move from simpler to more differentiated or complex forms.

Auguste Comte's Law of Three Stages (theological, metaphysical, positive) is an early evolutionary theory. Herbert Spencer described evolution from simple, homogeneous societies to complex, heterogeneous ones and used the phrase 'survival of the fittest'.

Lewis Henry Morgan, in 'Ancient Society' (1877), described three stages of human development: savagery, barbarism and civilization. Durkheim described a change from mechanical solidarity to organic solidarity as the division of labour increased.

Criticisms: early evolutionary theories assumed all societies follow the same path and treated Western society as the highest stage. Neo-evolutionists such as Talcott Parsons and Gerhard Lenski later offered more careful versions.
Functional approaches examine how social systems adjust when one institution or part of society changes. Change is understood in relation to adaptation and the maintenance of social order.

Talcott Parsons viewed society as a system in equilibrium. Change occurs when one part of the system changes, creating strain, and the system adjusts to restore balance. He described the processes of evolutionary change as differentiation, adaptive upgrading, inclusion and value generalization.
Robert K. Merton's idea of dysfunctions shows that some elements can create strain and lead to change.
Criticism: functional theory is said to explain stability better than change and to neglect conflict and power.
Conflict theories see social change as strongly influenced by inequalities, competing interests and struggles between social groups. Conflict can challenge existing institutions and power relations.

Karl Marx argued that 'the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (The Communist Manifesto, 1848). He saw change occurring through the conflict between classes, such as feudal lords and serfs or capitalists and workers, leading to new forms of society.

Ralf Dahrendorf, in 'Class and Class Conflict in Industrial Society' (1959), argued that conflict arises from unequal distribution of authority, not only property. Lewis Coser showed that conflict can have positive functions, such as promoting change and strengthening group solidarity.
Conflict theory helps explain social movements, revolutions, trade union struggles, caste movements and women's movements.
Cyclical theories suggest that societies or civilizations may pass through recurring phases of growth, maturity, decline and renewal rather than moving in a single straight line.

Oswald Spengler, in 'The Decline of the West' (1918-1922), compared civilizations to living organisms that pass through birth, growth, maturity and decay. He predicted the decline of Western civilization.

Arnold J. Toynbee, in 'A Study of History', explained the rise and fall of civilizations through 'challenge and response': civilizations grow when a creative minority responds successfully to challenges, and decline when they fail.

Pitirim Sorokin, in 'Social and Cultural Dynamics' (1937-1941), described societies fluctuating between ideational culture (based on faith and spiritual values), sensate culture (based on the senses and material values) and an intermediate idealistic culture. Vilfredo Pareto's theory of the 'circulation of elites' (between 'lions' and 'foxes') is also cyclical.
M. N. Srinivas used Sanskritization to describe a process in which a lower-status caste or group adopts practices and lifestyles associated with higher castes in an effort to improve social status.

Srinivas introduced the term in 'Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India' (1952). He first called it 'Brahminization' but later used Sanskritization because the reference model could also be Kshatriya, Vaishya or other locally dominant castes.

Sanskritization involves adopting practices such as vegetarianism, teetotalism, wearing the sacred thread, Sanskritic rituals and restrictions on widow remarriage. Srinivas noted that it leads to 'positional change' within the caste hierarchy, not a structural change in the system itself.

Critics pointed out that it can reinforce caste hierarchy and patriarchal practices. Yogendra Singh discussed it in 'Modernization of Indian Tradition' (1973), and some scholars have noted 'de-Sanskritization' movements that reject upper-caste models, such as the non-Brahmin movement in South India.
Westernization, in Srinivas's use, refers to changes in Indian society resulting from prolonged contact with Western, especially British, institutions, technology, education, values and ways of life.

Srinivas, in 'Social Change in Modern India' (1966), defined Westernization as 'the changes brought about in Indian society and culture as a result of over 150 years of British rule, the term subsuming changes occurring at different levels: technology, institutions, ideology and values'.
Westernization influenced dress, food habits, language (English), education, law, the press, railways, the bureaucracy, and values such as humanitarianism, rationalism and equality.

It was first adopted by upper castes and urban elites, then spread more widely. Sanskritization and Westernization could occur together, and Srinivas noted that Westernization also encouraged Sanskritization by spreading means of communication.
Secularization refers to a process in which areas of social life become less directly governed by religious authority or explanation. Its form and extent differ across societies.
Srinivas described secularization in India as a process in which 'what was previously regarded as religious is now ceasing to be such', with increased rationalism and differentiation of institutions.

Indicators of secularization include: the decline of religious control over education, law and politics; the rise of scientific explanation; the decline of purity-pollution rules in public places; and greater rationality in everyday life.

Secularization is different from secularism. Secularization is a social process; secularism is a political principle about the relationship between state and religion. In India, religion continues to play an important role in public life, so secularization has been partial.
Modernization refers to broad transformation associated with industrialization, urbanization, education, science, technology, bureaucratic organization and changing social values.

Modernization involves industrialization, urbanization, the spread of education and mass media, scientific outlook, democratic institutions, social mobility, and rational-legal bureaucracy. Daniel Lerner, in 'The Passing of Traditional Society' (1958), emphasized empathy and mobility as features of modern personality.

Yogendra Singh, in 'Modernization of Indian Tradition' (1973), argued that Indian modernization does not mean the complete replacement of tradition but an adaptive process in which tradition and modernity coexist.

Critics argued that early modernization theory equated modernity with Westernization and ignored the different paths of non-Western societies. Concepts such as 'multiple modernities' highlight these different paths.

sections.title: Nature and Characteristics of Social Change

blocks.text:
Social change refers to significant changes in social structure, institutions, relationships, norms or values over time. All societies change, although the speed, direction and extent of change vary.

Social change is continuous and universal but not uniform. It may be planned through policy and reform or arise unexpectedly through technology, conflict or crisis. Progress should not be confused with change because progress involves a value judgement that change is desirable. Development usually refers to broader economic, social and institutional transformation.

Evolution describes gradual cumulative change, while revolution involves rapid and fundamental transformation. Change may face obstacles such as rigid traditions, vested interests, inequality, lack of resources and resistance from groups that benefit from existing arrangements. Sociology studies both the forces producing change and the conditions that slow or redirect it.

Social change can be studied at different levels: micro (changes in individual attitudes and interaction), meso (changes in organizations and communities) and macro (changes in institutions and whole societies).
Patterns of change include linear (progress in one direction), cyclical (repeated cycles of rise and fall) and fluctuating (oscillation between opposite tendencies).

Planned social change in India has been pursued through the Five Year Plans, land reforms, Panchayati Raj, reservation, rural development programmes and social legislation. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.

In Mizoram, social change has been rapid since the late nineteenth century: conversion to Christianity, mission education, the decline of chieftainship (abolished in 1954), political mobilization, statehood (1987), urbanization and globalization have transformed society, though values such as tlawmngaihna continue.
In conclusion, social change is inevitable, but its direction and speed depend on the interaction of many factors and on human choices and policies.

Social change is produced by several interacting factors. Technology can transform production, transport, communication and everyday life. It can create new occupations and relationships while weakening older arrangements.

Education spreads knowledge and skills and influences values, aspirations and mobility. Cultural factors include changes in beliefs, values, ideas and contact between cultures. Economic factors such as industrialization, markets, employment and changes in property relations influence class structure, migration and family life.

No single factor explains every case of social change. Technological change may require education; economic change may influence cultural values; and cultural ideas may shape economic or political reform. Social change is therefore best understood as a multi-causal process.

Other factors include demographic factors (population growth, migration, age structure), biological factors, environmental and geographical factors (climate, natural disasters), political factors (laws, state policies, revolutions) and ideological factors (new ideas and social movements).

Theorists emphasize different factors: Marx emphasized economic factors; Weber emphasized religious and cultural ideas; Ogburn emphasized technology; and environmental determinists emphasized geography.

Most sociologists today adopt a multi-causal or pluralistic approach. For example, the changing status of women in India results from education, economic participation, legal reform, women's movements, media and technology working together.
Students should explain each factor with examples, and conclude that social change results from the interaction of several factors, not from a single cause.

The syllabus identifies evolutionary, functional, conflict and cyclical theories. Evolutionary theories explain change as gradual movement from simpler toward more differentiated forms of social organization.

Functional theories view society as an interrelated system. Change in one part creates pressures for adjustment in other parts, and institutions adapt in order to restore coordination or stability.

Conflict theories emphasize inequality and struggles between groups with different interests. Social change may occur when subordinate groups challenge existing distributions of power and resources. Cyclical theories reject the idea of continuous linear progress and suggest that societies or civilizations may experience recurring phases of rise, maturity and decline.

Each theory highlights a different dimension. Together they show that social change may involve development, adaptation, conflict and recurring historical patterns.
Evolutionary theory (Comte, Spencer, Morgan, Durkheim): change is gradual and moves from simple to complex. Criticism: it assumes a single path and Western superiority.

Functional theory (Parsons, Merton): society is a system that adjusts to maintain equilibrium; change happens through differentiation and adaptation. Criticism: it neglects conflict and sudden change.
Conflict theory (Marx, Dahrendorf, Coser): change results from struggles between groups over power and resources. Criticism: it may overemphasize conflict and economic factors.
Cyclical theory (Spengler, Toynbee, Sorokin, Pareto): societies pass through recurring cycles of growth and decline. Criticism: it is often speculative and difficult to test.
Each theory explains some aspects of social change. A comprehensive understanding combines insights from all of them.

sections.title: Processes of Social Change: Sanskritization, Westernization, Secularization and Modernization

blocks.text:
Sanskritization and Westernization are important concepts associated with M. N. Srinivas's analysis of Indian social change. Sanskritization describes the adoption by a lower-status caste or group of practices associated with higher castes in an effort to raise social status. Westernization refers to changes resulting from prolonged contact with Western, particularly British, institutions, education, technology and values.

Secularization refers broadly to a reduction in the direct control of religious authority over certain areas of social life and the increasing differentiation of social institutions. Modernization is a wider process involving industrialization, urbanization, education, science, technology, bureaucracy and changing values.

These processes are analytically different and may occur together or unevenly. They help sociologists understand how Indian society combines continuity of older institutions with new forms of social and cultural transformation.

Srinivas's concepts help explain change in caste society: Sanskritization explains mobility within the system, while Westernization explains change arising from British contact. Yogendra Singh distinguished between 'orthogenetic' change (from within the tradition) and 'heterogenetic' change (from contact with other cultures).
Secularization has affected education, law and public life, though religion remains important. Modernization involves the growth of science, technology, democracy, education and urbanization.

These processes often overlap. For example, a family may adopt modern education and occupations (Westernization and modernization), become less bound by ritual rules (secularization), and also adopt certain high-caste customs (Sanskritization).
In tribal societies of the North-East, such as the Mizo, change has come more through Christianization, mission education, Westernization and modernization than through Sanskritization.
In conclusion, Indian society shows a mixture of tradition and modernity. Students should define each process, mention its features and examples, discuss criticisms and show how they interact.
